name: Nora Kessling
equipment: .32 pocket pistol (Colt 1903, blued, bought on Tuesday from Elmer Dahl's pawnshop for $22), 8 rounds loaded, in her handbag
A cardboard folder: the photostat of the 1946 Lindqvist statement, her own typed copy for him to sign, and the Ledger clipping of her father's execution
A worn deck of cards that was her father's, which she shuffles when she is nervous
Her Ledger switchboard operator's headset and badge
A complimentary ticket to the Regent rally, balcony C-14, which arrived from the DA's office on Wednesday and which she thinks is a joke
A good grey suit, a cloche hat, a raincoat, and a pair of sensible shoes she has resoled twice
An IOU for $15 from a Courier reporter who lost to her at gin rummy and has not paid
Keys to her room at 14 Mercer Lane
features: Knows the Block (City-Born origin: she grew up on the Tin Mile and knows every alley, net loft, tavern and rooming house on it; advantage on Streetwise checks to find a person, place or service in the city)
The Long Con (Grifter: in downtime, a day and $20 builds a cover identity; she can keep two; she has been running one on Wendell Sloane since July, as an anonymous correspondent who knows everything)
Cheap Shot (Grifter: once per turn, an extra 2d6 damage with a finesse Melee weapon or a Sidearm when she has advantage, an ally is next to the target, or the target thinks she is harmless)
Quick Hands (Grifter, 2nd level: on each of her turns, a bonus action to Dash, Disengage or Hide, or to make one Sleight of Hand check to lift, plant or palm something)

Racket: Short Con (Grifter, 3rd level: Fast Talk: as an action, a creature that can hear and understand her makes a WIS save, DC 12, or loses its next reaction and has disadvantage on its next attack roll)
Ability Score Improvement (Grifter, 4th level: +1 Intelligence, +1 Charisma)
Back Room Game (Card Sharp background: she can find a card game anywhere in the city, read the players at it, and win or lose exactly as much as she means to; at a card table, people talk)

The Switchboard (personal: she works the Ledger switchboard and can listen to any call that goes through it; she knows who rings whom at the Ledger and, through the operators' grapevine, at the Courier and the Hall of Justice)

personality.traits: I listen with my head on one side and remember every word. I shuffle my father's cards when I am nervous, and I am nervous all the time this week. I am polite to everyone, and I am lying to almost all of them.
personality.ideals: The truth does not need to be kind, or useful, or safe. It just needs to be said, out loud, where people can hear it.
personality.bonds: My father, Daniel Kessling, who taught me gin rummy and the words to "Solidarity Forever" and how to tell when a man is bluffing, and whom the state of Port Calloway killed on 31 October 1947, when I was twenty-one. And my mother, who died of it two years later.
personality.flaws: I bought a gun on Tuesday. I told the man in the shop it was for protection. I do not know what I am going to do with it on Friday night, and I am more afraid of that than I am of Wendell Sloane.

appearance: A slim young woman of twenty-six with a pale, serious, pointed face, dark hair cut short under a cloche hat, her father's square jaw and grey eyes, and a way of standing very still and listening that makes people say more than they meant to. She dresses in one good grey suit she cannot afford to replace. She looks younger than she is, which she uses.
backstory: Nora Kessling grew up in two rooms on Mercer Lane on the Tin Mile, the only child of Daniel Kessling, the organizer of Local 9, and his wife Ingrid, a cannery packer from Malmö. She learned cards at union-hall poker games on her father's knee, and to keep a straight face from watching him negotiate with cannery owners. She was nineteen when the Halvorsen Cannery burned, twenty when her father was convicted, and twenty-one when she stood outside the penitentiary in the rain all night with a candle and a woman in a good coat she did not know held her hand. Her mother died in 1949. Nora has worked the Ledger switchboard since 1950, and in July 1952 an envelope came to her at the Ledger with no letter in it and a photostat of a statement she had never known existed, signed by the night watchman her father's lawyer could never find. She has spent the summer finding him, and the autumn deciding what to do. On Saturday 25 October she typed one word on the switchboard Underwood, pasted it under her father's obituary, and mailed it to the district attorney. She meant it as a promise, not a threat. She is beginning to understand that in Port Calloway there is no difference.

dmNotes.roleplaying: Nora is the heart of the campaign: the sender of the threat, the bait in Vantreight's frame, and the person with the most right to decide what happens to the truth. She should be met in glimpses in pa-scenario-001 (the switchboard, the pawnshop, a lit window), properly on the ferry in pa-scenario-002, and become a companion from then on if the party earns her trust. She is clever, brave, frightened and stubborn, and she will not be managed: she will stand up at the rally on Friday whatever anyone says, and the party's job is to make sure she is standing in the right place with the right thing in her hands. Never make her a damsel. She has agency and her own plan, and it is a good one; it just did not account for Vantreight.
dmNotes.voice: Low, clear, quick, with a Tin Mile directness and the operator's trick of sounding pleasant while saying no. Says 'Number, please' when she is being sarcastic. Quotes her father ('Dad used to say a boss never lies, he just remembers selectively'). When she talks about him her voice does not change at all, which is how you know.
dmNotes.motivations: Primary: say it out loud on Friday, the anniversary, in front of the whole city, so that it can never be unsaid. Secondary: get the Ledger to print it, with Lindqvist's signature. Tertiary, and secret even from herself: make Wendell Sloane afraid, the way her father must have been, for five days.
dmNotes.secrets: She does not know who sent her the photostat; she half suspects Miriam Holloway. It was Constance Sloane, the woman in the good coat at the vigil, and when Nora finds out (Iris Nakamura's 1947 negative, or Constance herself) it should be one of the campaign's quiet great scenes. Second secret: she has been listening to Sloane's office calls through the Hall of Justice operators' grapevine all week, and she knows he hired detectives. She knew who the party was before they ever came to the Ledger. Third: the gun. She has not decided. If nobody she trusts asks her to leave it at home on Friday, she takes it.
dmNotes.attitude: Toward the party: suspicion, then a careful, conditional trust, then fierce loyalty to whoever proves they are not Sloane's dogs. Toward Isaiah Bell: instant warmth; her father talked about him. Toward Iris Nakamura: a younger sister's trust. Toward Frank Lusk: contempt, which may become pity. Toward Sloane: a cold, steady hatred she is ashamed of. Toward Constance Sloane, once she knows: she does not know yet. That is the scene.
